Overall: 8.5/10.

Story & Plot

Set just after the Thirty Years' War in a 17th-century German Protestant village, a former soldier named Rose arrives claiming to be the heir to an abandoned farmstead. Inspired by documented accounts of women pretending to be men in Europe, Rose seeks to live a normal life with the privileges of a man. As the soldier attempts to settle down and buy a stream, the villagers' suspicions grow, ultimately forcing a reckoning.

Comedy & Entertainment

The film features a darkly funny exploration of identity and freedom rooted in its historical premise. While it is primarily an immaculately controlled folk tragedy, the clever subterfuge and subversion of patriarchal norms lend the narrative a sharp, understated entertainment value. It balances its tense agrarian setting with these witty undercurrents of gender privilege.

Performances & Direction

Sandra Hüller anchors the film with a blazing vitality, getting completely lost in her character's male persona with the aid of excellent prosthetics and make-up. Silently observant for much of the time, her performance is punctuated by startling moments of raging anger and distinct character tics. Supporting cast members such as Godehard Giese round out the ensemble in this sharp historical drama.

Strengths

  • Sandra Hüller's astonishing lead performance
  • Markus Schleinzer's confident direction
  • Striking black-and-white cinematography
  • A compelling exploration of gender privilege and historical tragedy

Weaknesses

While the film is told with confidence and brisk pacing, the heavy atmosphere and deceptive simplicity of the folk tragedy may test some viewers looking for faster narrative momentum. The looming historical weight and tragic shadow hanging over the narrative also mean the film resists traditional crowd-pleasing resolutions, keeping tension simmering rather than offering easy release.

Final verdict

Markus Schleinzer's Rose is a striking and immaculately controlled period drama that benefits immensely from Sandra Hüller's commanding lead performance. Blending historical tragedy with sharp social commentary, it stands as a worthwhile and provocative viewing experience. Recommended for fans of thoughtful historical dramas and masterclass acting.

A celebrated Olympian shooter travels to America in search of a donor to help his sick child, but an unexpected romance complicates his mission. Director Venky Atluri delivers an urbane, contemporary story centered on fun, emotions, childhood trauma, healing, and companionship. The family drama also touches on topics like marriage, parenting, and contrasting generations.

Comedy & Entertainment

The film offers an entertainment-filled treatment from end to end with witty dialogues and lighthearted proceedings. Reviewers note it is entertaining throughout and serves as a lovely family entertainer packed with fun. Characters bring the house down with their antics, making it a humorous watch for family audiences and youngsters alike.

Suriya delivers a brilliant, age-appropriate performance as Sanju, with his charm holding the warm film together.   • Grand production values
  • Witty dialogues and emotional depth

The film suffers from a dip during Raveena Tandon's thread and a slower second half packed with sentimental scenes. With no big bad villains in the picture, the fight sequences feel very unnecessary and the overall plot is considered weak by some.

Vishwanath and Sons is a heartwarming, feel-good family drama that offers a breezy exploration of relationships with plenty of charm. While it has a weaker plot and a slower second half, the strong performances and entertaining treatment make it a must-watch with the whole family.

An intimate portrait of two people bound by love, ambition, and the pursuit of the impossible. Elite ski mountaineers Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson fell deeply in love while reaching the pinnacle of their sport. Their drive sharpened into a shared dream: to climb and ski the direct North Face of Mount Everest—the most difficult and dangerous climb on the mountain and the most coveted ski line on Earth—something only a handful have ever achieved, and no one has successfully skied down.

Story & Plot

The documentary Everest: The Other Side follows elite ski mountaineers Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson as they pursue a shared dream. Bound by love and ambition, they aim to climb and ski down the direct North Face of Mount Everest, the most dangerous climb on the mountain and a line no one has successfully skied down before. Filmmakers Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi capture this harrowing high-altitude journey of risk-takers facing chancing death and the complex spectrum of grief and obsession.

Comedy & Entertainment

As a documentary focusing on extreme high-altitude mountaineering and tragic risk-taking, the film does not feature traditional comedy or lighthearted humor. Its entertainment value relies instead on the tense, high-stakes premise of climbing the world's most dangerous mountain face. Viewers looking for levity will find none, as the narrative maintains a serious and heavy tone throughout.

Performances & Direction

The documentary features real-life subjects and mountain climbers including Hilaree Nelson, Jim Morrison, Jimmy Chin, Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, and Mikey Schaefer. Reviewers note that the subjects' extreme compulsions and personal choices create a heavy watch, with Morrison's drive pulling him into a mournful and solitary march. The participants display fierce snow determination and vulnerability in the face of immense danger.

Strengths

  • Impressive cinematography
  • Inspiring and harrowing story
  • Engaging narrative structure
  • High-altitude risk-taking focus

Weaknesses

The documentary suffers from uneven editing that makes the narrative choppy and occasionally disjointed. Additionally, the film becomes a mournful and increasingly solitary march as extreme compulsions pull the focus toward a disquieting and heavy second half.

Final verdict

Everest: The Other Side is a harrowing and visually impressive documentary about the dangers and obsessions of elite mountain climbing. While uneven editing and a heavy second half make it a challenging watch, it offers an intimate and gripping portrait of ambition. It is recommended for viewers interested in high-altitude survival stories and extreme mountaineering.
